title: Sleep and Recovery
summary: Anchor the wake time → Count back → Set up the room → Test for seven days
subtitle: Plan rest backwards from the alarm, so movement fits the life you actually have.

blocks.text: A fitness app may send a cheerful workout reminder at the exact moment you finally sit down. Its calendar has never worked a late shift or settled a child after midnight. Rest deserves space in your plan, even when the reminder has excellent graphics.

Everything in this course so far has asked your body to do something: walk, lift, stretch, punch the air. This lesson is about the part that makes all of it work. Muscles, balance and mood improve during recovery, not during the workout itself. Skip the recovery, and the workouts stop paying off.

Here’s the twist. Most sleep advice starts with bedtime, but bedtime is the part of your day you control least. Your alarm is usually fixed by work, school runs or a care schedule. So this lesson starts at the other end. You’ll pick your wake-up time first and count backwards to find everything else.
Wake up more ready for your day.
blocks.detail: Knowing how much rest you need, and protecting it, makes every other healthy habit easier to keep.
blocks.extra: Section 03 turns your wake-up time into a lights-out time you can protect.

blocks.text: Recovery means giving yourself time and support to feel ready again after activity and everyday demands. Sleep is part of recovery, along with breaks, meals, water and manageable movement. A hard workday counts when you decide how much extra activity fits.

The time you set aside for sleep is your sleep opportunity. The time you’re asleep can be shorter, since falling asleep and waking in the night use some of it. That gap is why the plan in Section 03 adds settling time on top of the sleep you’re aiming for.
What Canada’s guidelines say

items.title: Adults 18–64
items.text: 7 to 9 hours — of good-quality sleep a night, with steady bedtimes and wake-up times.

items.title: Adults 65+
items.text: 7 to 8 hours — of good-quality sleep a night, with steady bedtimes and wake-up times.

items.title: In bed vs asleep
items.text: 8 h ≠ 8 h — Eight hours in bed doesn’t mean eight hours of sleep. Settling and night waking use some of it.

blocks.text: Your work or caregiving schedule may need its own pattern. A night-shift worker sleeps in the day. A parent of a baby has broken nights. The ranges still apply, but the window moves, and that’s fine.
Protect a window, not a score. Write down when sleep could fit before you buy a tracker. A device can’t create time that work and caregiving have already used up.

items.title: Rest that never gets a time slot never happens.
items.text: Rest that never gets a time slot never happens.

items.title: Fix the wake-up time, then count back.
items.text: Fix the wake-up time, then count back.

blocks.text: Your wake-up time is your anchor. It’s the one time most days that won’t move, so build everything else from it. The maths has three parts: the sleep you’re aiming for, the minutes it usually takes you to fall asleep and the wind-down that comes before lights out.
Wake-up time − (hours of sleep + minutes to fall asleep) = lights-out time. Then subtract your wind-down to find when to start getting ready.

Here’s a worked example. The alarm is set for 6:30 a.m. You’re aiming for 7 hours 30 minutes of sleep, and it usually takes you about 20 minutes to drift off. 6:30 a.m. − 7 hours 50 minutes = 10:40 p.m. lights out. A 15-minute wind-down starts at 10:25 p.m. If you stop caffeine about six hours before lights out, your last coffee is around 4:40 p.m.
Find your lights-out time
blocks.extra: Enter your fixed wake-up time and the sleep you’re aiming for. The plan counts back for you.

blocks.text: Now read the answer honestly. If the plan says lights out at 9:10 p.m. and your shift ends at 9 p.m., the maths isn’t wrong. It’s telling you something has to move: the commute, a chore, the evening scroll or the wake-up time itself. That’s a schedule question, not a willpower question.

Try to keep your wake-up time close to the same on days off. A long lie-in feels like a reward, but it pushes your body clock later, and Sunday night gets harder. The day-off example above wakes only an hour later than the workday one, which is a gentler shift.

items.title: “I’ll catch up on sleep at the weekend.”
items.text: A longer sleep can ease some tiredness, but it doesn’t undo a short week, and a very late wake-up makes the next night harder. A steady window does more.

sections.title: Set up the room and the evening

blocks.text: A lights-out time only helps if the room and the evening let you use it. You don’t need a new mattress or a gadget before trying a small fix. Pick the one change below that you can afford this week.
Six levers for a better sleep window

items.title: Dark room
items.text: Close the blind, cover small lights and check that curtains actually meet. Daytime sleepers need this most.

items.title: Quiet
items.text: Ask others to keep the noise down at set times, or try a fan or earplugs.

items.title: Comfortable temperature
items.text: A slightly cool room helps most people settle. Adjust layers before buying anything new.

items.title: Stopping point
items.text: Pack tomorrow’s lunch, leave a note for an unfinished chore and move work messages out of reach.

items.title: Caffeine cut-off
items.text: Its effects last for hours, so many people stop about six hours before lights out.

items.title: Go easy on alcohol
items.text: A drink can make you sleepy at first, then wake you up more during the night.

blocks.text: Health Canada suggests adults have no more than 400 mg of caffeine a day, about three small cups of brewed coffee. Energy drinks, strong tea and some pain relievers count too. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about medicine concerns instead of changing a prescription yourself.

items.title: “Alcohol is a reliable sleep aid.”
items.text: Feeling sleepy after a drink doesn’t mean your sleep will be restful. Alcohol can make you wake up more during the night.

sections.title: Let recovery steer the movement plan

blocks.text: Recovery belongs in your movement plan too. Before you start, decide which kind of day it is: your usual session, an easier version or rest. Make that call based on the night you had and the day ahead, not on what the app scheduled.

After a short night or a demanding shift, choose a shorter familiar activity instead of adding another hard session. Regular meals and water are part of recovery, no supplements required. For example, pack your usual sandwich and fruit for after a walk after work, and bring water.
Make the easier option specific. “Walk gently for five minutes if it feels comfortable” is a clearer backup than “do something.” Taking a rest day is a valid choice too.

Low energy is different from pain or injury, which you shouldn’t push through. Tiredness that lifts after a few minutes of easy movement is normal. Pain that sharpens or a body that feels worse as you go is your signal to stop.

items.title: “A missed workout must be added to tomorrow.”
items.text: Doubling the next session can crowd out recovery. Go back to a manageable plan instead.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Keep a simple indoor option for icy paths, extreme cold or smoky summer air. Checking local conditions before an outdoor session saves you getting ready for a route you can’t use.

Choose one sleep window that fits tomorrow’s duties, then get ready for it. Treat the plan below as an example you can adjust, not a personal prescription. It doesn’t ask you to sleep less or force yourself to sleep on command.
Adjustable 15-minute wind-down example

items.title: Minutes 0–5: finish one needed preparation, such as setting out work clothes
Minutes 5–8: lower room light and put non-urgent messages aside
Minutes 8–15: read something quiet or listen to gentle music
Total: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15 minutes before your planned sleep window

blocks.text: If fifteen minutes doesn’t fit, try five minutes for one helpful step. Keep essential caregiving or emergency contacts within reach. The routine is an invitation to settle down, not a test you fail if you stay awake.
Seven days, one change

items.title: OBSERVE
items.text: Privately note your planned window, a rough guess at your sleep if it helps and how ready you feel for everyday tasks.

items.title: ONE CHANGE
items.text: Try one change from the six levers, like a darker room or an earlier caffeine cut-off. Keep everything else the same.

items.title: REVIEW
items.text: Compare the two halves of the week. Note what helped, what didn’t and what still needs support from someone else.

items.title: REPEAT
items.text: Keep the change that helped and test the next one, or repeat the same week if the first one was unusual.

blocks.text: Change one thing at a time. Keeping the rest of your plan the same makes it easier to tell whether the change helps.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The curtain note

blocks.text: The curtain note
paragraphs: Mara worked rotating shifts at a food plant in Saskatoon. She wanted enough energy to join her sister’s Saturday walks without spending the afternoon on the couch. Her kitchen calendar had walking dates on it, but no space marked for rest.

After three late shifts in a row, Mara slept through their meeting time. Her sister’s message was kind, but Mara worried their weekly time together would fade away. Before agreeing to another early start, she decided to look at her week.

She counted back from a 3 p.m. alarm: 7 hours 30 minutes of sleep plus 20 minutes to settle meant lights out by 7:10 a.m. For seven days, she noted that window and how rested she felt. Laundry and grocery runs kept eating it. A longer walk wouldn’t fix that.

She called her sister and moved the walk to the afternoon. She asked her roommate to leave the laundry until she woke up. After late shifts, she chose a ten-minute easy walk instead of her usual longer route.

The first protected morning still went badly, because sunlight spilled past the bedroom curtain. Her roommate saw the note asking for quiet and pointed out that the curtain had slipped off one hook. Fixing it took two minutes, which beat the new blackout curtains Mara had started pricing.

The next week was mixed, with one surprise shift change. Mara kept two planned sleep windows and joined the shorter Saturday walk. She didn’t pretend every tired day was gone. Beside the next walking date, she wrote “rest window” and drew a tiny curtain hook.

items.title: 3 P.M. ALARM
items.text: Lights out by 7:10 a.m.

items.title: SEVEN DAYS
items.text: Laundry ate the window

items.title: TWO MINUTES
items.text: Curtain back on its hook

blocks.text: Ask for a clear change. A request like “Could the laundry wait until I wake up on Tuesday?” gives someone an easy way to help.
One small fix can protect a lot of rest.
blocks.detail: A practical change to your schedule or space makes rest easier to keep, without rebuilding your whole life.
blocks.extra: Section 08 shows when rest needs more than a plan.

blocks.text: This lesson is general learning, not insomnia treatment or a medical plan. A better window and a darker room help a lot of people, but some sleep problems need a professional. Knowing the difference is part of an Elite plan.

items.title: STOP AND GET HELP
list: Never drive while drowsy. Pull over somewhere safe or arrange another ride.
Stop movement for new pain, dizziness, chest discomfort or unusual breathlessness, and get appropriate care.

items.title: TALK TO A CLINICIAN
list: Sleep trouble that lasts, even with a steady window.
Loud snoring with pauses in breathing.
Daytime sleepiness that gets in the way of daily tasks.
For long-lasting insomnia, the first treatment doctors usually recommend is a type of coaching called CBT-I, not sleeping pills.

items.title: WHO ELSE CAN HELP
list: A pharmacist, for questions about how a medicine or caffeine might affect your sleep.
Your provincial health line, 811 in most provinces, for advice on what kind of care fits.

blocks.text: Quick Check

items.title: Your alarm is 7:00 a.m. You’re aiming for 8 hours of sleep and usually take 15 minutes to fall asleep. When is lights out?
items.text: 7:00 a.m. − (8 hours + 15 minutes) = 10:45 p.m.

items.title: Lights out is 11:00 p.m. Using the six-hour guide, when is your last caffeine?
You spend 8 hours in bed and are awake for about 40 minutes of it. Roughly how long did you sleep?
items.text: 8 hours − 40 minutes = 7 hours 20 minutes. Time in bed isn’t the same as time asleep.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Lee has eight hours available for sleep but is awake for part of it. Which is accurate? A. Lee certainly slept eight hours. · B. Sleep opportunity and actual sleep can differ. · C. Lee must exercise longer.
items.text: Time available includes time awake, so it cannot confirm the amount slept.

items.title: Priya’s alarm is 5:30 a.m. She aims for 7.5 hours and takes 20 minutes to settle, so lights out is 9:40 p.m. Her dishes usually run until 9:45 p.m. What fits this lesson? A. Cut her sleep to 7 hours. · B. Move the dishes earlier or ask for help. · C. Skip the wind-down every night.
items.text: The count-back shows a schedule clash. Moving the task protects the window instead of shrinking it.

items.title: Sam finishes a tiring shift before a planned walk. What fits this lesson? A. Double the walking time. · B. Ignore new pain. · C. Choose an easier version or rest.
items.text: Daily demands matter when choosing activity; pain should not be pushed through.

items.title: Jo hears that their partner snores loudly and has breathing pauses. What should Jo suggest? A. Get clinician advice. · B. Diagnose the cause from a tracker. · C. Try alcohol before sleep.
items.text: Breathing pauses need professional advice, and this course cannot identify the cause.

blocks.text: Anchor your wake-up time, count back to a lights-out time you can protect, change one thing at a time, and let your movement plan include easier days and rest.
Write your own small recovery plan below. Start with your wake-up time and count back. Keep detailed sleep notes and private health information in your own notebook.
Check that your plan names a step you can take, not a result you must achieve.

items.title: Wake-time anchor
items.text: A wake-up time you keep steady and plan the rest of your sleep around.

items.title: Lights-out time
items.text: The time you aim to be in bed with the lights off, found by counting back from your wake-up time.

items.title: Sleep opportunity
items.text: Time you have made available for sleep.

items.title: Actual sleep
items.text: Time spent asleep within that opportunity.

items.title: Wind-down
items.text: A short routine to help you settle before sleep.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: Time and support after activity or daily demands.

items.title: CBT-I
items.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, a coaching-based treatment for long-lasting sleep trouble.

items.title: Drowsy
items.text: Sleepy enough that staying alert is difficult.
